column4: As Christendom today is divided into separate sects, denominations, or belief structures, so too, were the Jews of Jesus' age divided. During the time of Jesus, four major Jewish sects shaped the religious and political landscape of Israel, each with distinct beliefs and expectations about the Messiah. Understanding some background on these different groups can help provide meaningful context to a study of the New Testament scriptures.
column5: Just as the Christian world today is divided into denominations and sects or distinct doctrinal frameworks, so too were the Jews of Jesus’ time divided. In the time of Jesus, four major Jewish sects shaped the religious and political landscape of Israel, each with distinctive beliefs and expectations regarding the Messiah. Understanding some background about these different groups can help provide meaningful context for studying the books of the New Testament.

column4: The **Pharisees** were the most influential among the common people, known for their strict adherence to the Law (Torah) and oral traditions. They believed in the resurrection, the afterlife, and the existence of angels, emphasizing personal piety and obedience to God's commandments. Their messianic expectation was centered on a figure who would uphold the Law, bring justice, and restore Israel both politically and religiously.
column5: The **Pharisees** were the most influential among the common people, known for their strict adherence to the Law (Torah) and the oral traditions. They believed in the resurrection, life after death, and the existence of angels, and they emphasized personal piety and obedience to God’s commandments. Their messianic expectations centered on a figure who upheld the Law, brought justice, and restored Israel’s glory both politically and religiously.

column4: The **Sadducees**, in contrast, were a wealthy and politically powerful group that controlled the Temple and priesthood. They rejected oral traditions and accepted only the Torah as authoritative scripture. The Sadducees denied the resurrection, afterlife, and the existence of angels, focusing instead on maintaining their power and collaborating with Rome to ensure political stability. Consequently, they had little emphasis on a Messiah, as their primary concern was preserving the status quo.
column5: The **Sadducees**, by contrast, were a wealthy, politically influential group that controlled the Temple and the priesthood. The Sadducees denied the resurrection, life after death, and the existence of angels, focusing instead on preserving their power and cooperating with Rome to ensure political stability. Consequently, they did not place great importance on the Messiah, as their chief concern was maintaining the status quo.

column4: The **Essenes** were a separatist group that withdrew from mainstream Jewish society, living in isolated communities such as Qumran. They were deeply focused on ritual purity, apocalyptic expectations, and a disciplined lifestyle. The Essenes believed in two Messianic figures: a priestly Messiah who would restore the Temple's sanctity and a kingly Messiah who would lead Israel in righteousness. This dual-Messiah concept reflected their hope for a spiritual and political renewal. The Essenes are not directly referenced in the scriptures.

column4: Finally, the **Zealots** were militant nationalists who sought to overthrow Roman rule through violent rebellion. column4: The book of Hebrews explains at great length across its 13 chapters how Jesus became the perfect sacrifice, and was both the offering for sin, and the High Priest to offer it (Hebrews 3 & 4). The priesthood of Jesus is not of the Levitical line (after the tribe of Levi), but was in the manner of Melchizedek, who is said to have no beginning or end, meaning it’s not constrained to the patterns and habits of men (Hebrews 7:3). The limitation of the Levitical priesthood is that it depends on the blood of bulls and goats (Hebrews 9:12-13) whose sacrifice is insufficient for the permanent and lasting remission of sins. From our study on sin and sacrifice, we know that the consequence for sins of the people could be put off for a year (Hebrews 10:3) during the day of atonement, but that this sacrifice had to be renewed constantly.
column5: The Epistle to the Hebrews explains at length across its thirteen chapters how Jesus became the perfect sacrifice, and how He Himself was the offering for sin, and also the High Priest who presents it (Hebrews 3 & 4). Jesus’ priesthood is not from the Levitical tribe (according to the tribe of Levi), but according to the order of Melchizedek, who is said to be without beginning or end, that is, not bound by the patterns and customs of men (Hebrews 7:3). The limitation of the Levitical priesthood is that it relies on the blood of bulls and goats (Hebrews 9:12-13), whose sacrifices are not sufficient for a permanent and abiding forgiveness of sins. And from our study of sin and sacrifice we know that the consequences of the people’s sins could be postponed for one year (Hebrews 10:3) on the Day of Atonement, but that sacrifice had to be renewed continually.

column4: When we were born on the earth (born of flesh and water) many things occurred: we took our first breaths and were pronounced alive, we were received by our parents, were given a name, became an heir, received nourishment and protection, and continued to grow.
column5: When we were born on earth (born of the flesh and water) many things happened: we took our first breaths and it was declared that we are alive، our parents welcomed us، we were given a name، we became heirs، we received nourishment and protection، and we continued to grow.

column4: When we put our trust in Jesus and receive him, we become born again, not of flesh, but of the spirit. We become alive spiritually! Just as in physical birth, many things accompany spiritual birth:
column5: When we place our trust in Jesus and accept Him، we become born again، not of the flesh، but of the Spirit. We become spiritually alive! And as in physical birth، many things accompany spiritual birth:

column4: 1. When we accepted Jesus, God wiped away our sins and declared us forgiven (**justified**). He gave us a fresh start. The dividing wall between us and Him is removed. (Titus 3:5)
column5: 1. When we accepted Jesus، God erased our sins and declared that we are forgiven (**justified**). He granted us a fresh start. The dividing wall between us and Him was removed. (Titus 3:5)

column4: 2. We became spiritually **regenerated** and received the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. (1 Corinthians 6:19).
column5: 2. We became **renewed** spiritually and received the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. (1 Corinthians 6:19).

column4: 3. We became **adopted** into the family of God and became heirs. (Ephesians 1:5)
column5: 3. We became **adopted** into the family of God and became heirs. (Ephesians 1:5)

column4: 4. We receive a source of spiritual nourishment, and eternal protection. (1 Peter 2:2)
